summary: This program builds a list of Book objects for a small library, then walks that list to collect each book's genre into a second list of strings and prints them. It shows how one collection can be used to build another.

lines.text: ArrayList is the everyday, resizable list implementation in Java; it must be imported before it can be used.
List is the interface that describes what any list can do, and it is imported so variables can be declared with that general type.

The variable is typed as List<Book> but holds an ArrayList, a common Java habit that keeps the code tied to the general behaviour rather than one implementation. The <Book> part promises the list will only ever hold Book objects.
Creating the object and adding it to the list are two separate steps; at this point Eragon exists but the library does not know about it yet.
add() appends the book to the end of the list, so the list keeps insertion order and now has a fourth entry.
A second list is declared, this time holding String values, because genres are plain text rather than whole books.
This enhanced for loop hands you each Book in turn without any index bookkeeping, which is the usual way to read through a collection.
Each book is asked for its genre and that text is appended to the genres list, transforming a list of books into a list of strings.
The \n escape sequence prints a blank line before the heading, separating this section of output from anything printed earlier.
Looping over the new list proves it was filled correctly; note that "Fantasy" appears three times because a list allows duplicates.
Concatenating a dash in front of each value formats the output as a simple bulleted list.
